name: Force (F = ma)
description: Applies Newton's second law, F=mass×acceleration, to find the net force on an object in newtons from its mass in kg and acceleration in m/s².
notes: This gives the net (resultant) force. Use SI units (kg, m/s²) so the result is in newtons; force acts in the direction of acceleration.

name: Kinetic energy
description: Computes translational kinetic energy as ½×mass×velocity², giving the energy of motion in joules from mass in kg and speed in m/s.
notes: Velocity is squared, so doubling speed quadruples the energy. Use m/s for velocity; the result assumes non-relativistic (everyday) speeds.

name: Potential energy
description: Computes gravitational potential energy as mass×g×height, the energy stored by lifting a mass to a given height, in joules.
notes: Height is measured from your chosen reference level. Near Earth's surface g≈9.81 m/s²; the value is only accurate for modest heights.

name: Newton's second law (F=ma)
description: Applies Newton's second law F=m×a to find the net force in newtons from mass in kg and acceleration in m/s². Force and acceleration point in the same direction.
notes: Gives the net force producing the acceleration. Use SI units (kg and m/s²) for a result in newtons; this describes the resultant of all forces.

name: Final velocity (v = u + at)
description: Computes the final velocity under constant acceleration as u+a×t, from initial velocity u, acceleration a and elapsed time t. It is a standard equation of motion.
notes: Valid only for constant (uniform) acceleration. Use consistent signs: a negative acceleration (deceleration) reduces the velocity over time.

name: Displacement (s = ut + ½at²)
description: Computes displacement under constant acceleration as u×t+½×a×t², the distance travelled from initial velocity u over time t while accelerating at a.
notes: Valid only for constant acceleration. The result is displacement (net position change) along the direction of motion, which can be negative.

name: Velocity from displacement (v = √(u²+2as))
description: Computes the final speed after a displacement s under constant acceleration, using √(u²+2×a×s), from initial velocity u. This equation of motion contains no time term.
notes: Valid only for constant acceleration. If u²+2as is negative the motion cannot reach that displacement and the square root has no real value.

name: Average velocity ((u+v)/2)
description: Computes average velocity as the mean of initial and final velocity, (u+v)÷2. This shortcut holds only when acceleration is constant.
notes: Valid only for uniform acceleration, where velocity changes linearly with time. It does not apply when acceleration varies during the interval.

name: Free fall distance (h = ½gt²)
description: Computes the distance fallen from rest under gravity as ½×g×t², from gravitational acceleration g and fall time t. The result is the drop height in metres.
notes: Assumes the object starts from rest with no air resistance. Real falls with drag fall shorter than this ideal value, especially over long times.

name: Free fall velocity (v = gt)
description: Computes the speed of an object falling from rest under gravity after a given time, as the product of gravitational acceleration g and elapsed time t. The result is the instantaneous speed in metres per second.
notes: Assumes the object starts from rest and air resistance is negligible; near Earth's surface g is about 9.81 m/s². Time must be in seconds, giving speed in m/s.

name: Projectile range
description: Gives the horizontal distance a projectile travels over level ground, from its launch speed v and launch angle theta, using v² sin(2θ)/g. The result is the range in metres.
notes: The angle theta must be in radians and air resistance is ignored. Launch and landing heights are assumed equal; maximum range occurs at 45 degrees (about 0.785 rad).

name: Projectile maximum height
description: Computes the peak height a projectile reaches above its launch point, from the vertical component of its launch velocity, using (v sinθ)²/(2g). The result is the maximum height in metres.
notes: The angle theta must be in radians and air resistance is neglected. Only the vertical velocity component contributes; height is measured relative to the launch point.

name: Projectile time of flight
description: Gives the total time a projectile stays in the air over level ground, from its launch speed and angle, using 2v sinθ/g. The result is the flight time in seconds.
notes: The angle theta must be in radians and air resistance is ignored. Assumes launch and landing at the same height; this is twice the time to reach peak height.

name: Angular velocity (ω = v/r)
description: Computes the angular velocity of an object in circular motion, relating its linear speed v and radius r as v/r. The result is how fast it sweeps angle, in radians per second.
notes: The output is in radians per second, not revolutions; multiply by r to recover linear speed. Valid for motion on a circle of constant radius.

name: Angular velocity from period (ω = 2π/T)
description: Computes the angular velocity of uniform circular or periodic motion from its period T, as 2π/T. The result is the angular velocity in radians per second.
notes: The period t is the time for one full revolution, in seconds; the constant tau equals 2π. A shorter period gives a larger angular velocity.

name: Centripetal acceleration (a = ω²r)
description: Computes the centripetal acceleration of an object in circular motion from its angular velocity w and radius r, as ω²r. The result is the inward acceleration in m/s².
notes: Angular velocity w must be in radians per second; this form is equivalent to v²/r since v = ωr. The acceleration points toward the centre.

name: Kinetic energy (½mv²)
description: Computes the translational kinetic energy of a mass m moving at speed v, as ½mv². The result is the energy of motion in joules.
notes: Energy scales with the square of speed, so doubling speed quadruples it. Mass in kilograms and speed in m/s give joules; this is translational energy only.

name: Gravitational potential energy (mgh)
description: Computes the gravitational potential energy of a mass m raised to height h in a uniform gravitational field, as mgh. The result is the stored energy in joules.
notes: Height h is measured from a chosen reference level, so only differences in energy are physically meaningful. Valid near Earth's surface where g is roughly constant.

name: Momentum (p = mv)
description: Computes the linear momentum of a mass m moving at velocity v, as the product mv. The result is the momentum in kilogram-metres per second.
notes: Momentum is a vector sharing the direction of the velocity; a sign on v indicates its direction. It is conserved in the absence of external forces.

name: Impulse (J = FΔt)
description: Computes the impulse delivered by a constant force f acting over a time interval t, as the product ft. The result equals the change in momentum, in newton-seconds.
notes: Assumes the force is constant over the interval; for varying forces use the average force. Impulse equals the change in momentum and has the same units as momentum.

name: Impulse–momentum (F = mΔv/Δt)
description: Computes the average force needed to change a mass m's velocity by dv over a time interval t, as m·dv/t. The result is the average force in newtons.
notes: This gives the average force over the interval, not the instantaneous peak. Velocity change dv is a signed quantity; a shorter time for the same change means a larger force.

name: Power (P = W/t)
description: Computes the average power as the work done divided by the time taken, work/t. The result is the rate of energy transfer in watts.
notes: This yields average power over the interval; work in joules and time in seconds give watts (one watt is one joule per second).

name: Power (P = Fv)
description: Computes the instantaneous mechanical power delivered by a force f acting on a body moving at velocity v, as the product fv. The result is the power in watts.
notes: Strictly valid when force and velocity are parallel; otherwise use their component along the motion. Force in newtons and velocity in m/s give watts.

name: Work (W = Fd cosθ)
description: Computes the work done by a constant force f over a displacement d, accounting for the angle theta between them, as f·d·cosθ. The result is the work in joules.
notes: The angle theta must be in radians; work is zero when force is perpendicular to displacement and negative when it opposes the motion.

name: Friction force (f = μN)
description: Computes the friction force between two surfaces as the product of the friction coefficient mu and the normal force n. The result is the friction force in newtons.
notes: The coefficient mu is dimensionless; use the static value for maximum friction before sliding and the kinetic value while sliding. Friction is independent of contact area here.

name: Force along incline (mg sinθ)
description: Computes the component of gravity acting down a frictionless incline on a mass m, as mg sinθ, where theta is the incline angle. The result is the accelerating force in newtons.
notes: The angle theta must be in radians, measured from the horizontal; this ignores friction. As the slope steepens toward 90 degrees this component approaches the full weight.

name: Normal force on incline (mg cosθ)
description: Computes the normal (perpendicular) force from an incline on a mass m, as mg cosθ, where theta is the incline angle. The result is the support force in newtons.
notes: The angle theta must be in radians, measured from the horizontal. On a flat surface (theta = 0) this equals the full weight; it decreases as the slope steepens.

name: Torque (τ = rF sinθ)
description: Computes the torque produced by a force f applied at a lever arm r, with angle theta between them, as r·f·sinθ. The result is the turning effect in newton-metres.
notes: The angle theta must be in radians; torque is maximal when force is perpendicular to the lever arm (theta = π/2) and zero when parallel.

name: Hooke's law (F = kx)
description: Computes the restoring force of an ideal spring stretched or compressed by x, as the product of spring constant k and displacement x. The result is the force in newtons.
notes: Valid only within the spring's elastic limit where force is proportional to displacement; the actual restoring force opposes the displacement.

name: Elastic potential energy (½kx²)
description: Computes the elastic potential energy stored in a spring displaced by x from equilibrium, as ½kx². The result is the stored energy in joules.
notes: Valid within the elastic limit; energy grows with the square of displacement, so doubling x quadruples the stored energy. Displacement x is measured from equilibrium.

name: Mechanical advantage (MA = L/E)
description: Computes the mechanical advantage of a simple machine as the load force divided by the effort force. The result is a dimensionless factor showing how much the machine multiplies force.
notes: A value above 1 means the machine multiplies the applied force; the result is unitless as both inputs are forces. It reflects force ratio, not efficiency or energy.

name: Simple pendulum period (T = 2π√(L/g))
description: Computes the period of a simple pendulum of length l under gravity g, as 2π√(l/g). The result is the time for one complete swing, in seconds.
notes: Valid for small swing angles where the motion is approximately simple harmonic; the period is independent of the bob's mass. The constant tau equals 2π.

name: Mass-spring period (T = 2π√(m/k))
description: Computes the oscillation period of a mass m on a spring of stiffness k, as 2π√(m/k). The result is the time for one full oscillation, in seconds.
notes: Assumes an ideal, massless spring within its elastic limit and no damping; a stiffer spring or lighter mass gives a shorter period. The constant tau equals 2π.

name: Newton's law of gravitation
description: Computes the gravitational attraction between two masses m1 and m2 separated by distance r, as G·m1·m2/r². The result is the mutual force in newtons.
notes: The force weakens with the square of separation r, measured between centres of mass. Here g is the gravitational constant (about 6.674e-11 N·m²/kg²), not surface gravity.

name: Work done by a force
description: Computes the work done by a constant force f over a displacement d, with angle theta between them, as f·d·cosθ. The result is the energy transferred, in joules.
notes: The angle theta must be in radians; work is zero when the force is perpendicular to the displacement and negative when it opposes the motion.

name: Power (work over time)
description: Computes the average power as the work done w divided by the elapsed time t. The result is the rate of energy transfer in watts.
notes: This is average power over the interval; work in joules and time in seconds give watts (one watt equals one joule per second).

name: Gravitational field strength
description: Computes the gravitational field strength (acceleration due to gravity) at distance r from a body of mass m, as G·m/r². The result is the field strength in m/s².
notes: Distance r is measured from the body's centre and the field weakens with r². The constant gc is the gravitational constant (about 6.674e-11 N·m²/kg²).

name: Escape velocity
description: Computes the minimum speed needed to escape a body of mass m from radius r without further propulsion, as √(2Gm/r). The result is the escape velocity in metres per second.
notes: Ignores atmospheric drag and the body's rotation; it is independent of the escaping object's mass. Radius r is measured from the centre of the attracting body.

name: Orbital velocity
description: Computes the speed needed for a circular orbit at radius r around a central mass m, as √(Gm/r). The result is the orbital velocity in metres per second.
notes: Assumes a circular orbit and that the central mass dominates; orbital radius r is measured from its centre. Larger orbits correspond to slower orbital speeds.

name: Orbital period (Kepler)
description: Computes the period of a circular orbit at radius r around a central mass m, as 2π√(r³/(Gm)). The result is the time for one orbit, in seconds.
notes: This is Kepler's third law for a circular orbit; the period grows with r^1.5 and is independent of the orbiting body's mass. Radius r is from the centre.

name: Simple pendulum period
description: Computes the period of a simple pendulum of length l under gravity g, as 2π√(l/g). The result is the time for one complete swing, in seconds.
notes: Valid for small swing angles where the motion is approximately simple harmonic; the period does not depend on the bob's mass or amplitude.

name: Mass-spring period
description: Computes the oscillation period of a mass m on a spring of stiffness k, as 2π√(m/k). The result is the time for one full oscillation, in seconds.
notes: Assumes an ideal massless spring within its elastic limit and no damping; a stiffer spring or lighter mass shortens the period.

name: SHM displacement
description: Computes the displacement of a simple-harmonic oscillator at time t, as A cos(ωt), for amplitude a and angular frequency omega. The result is the position in metres.
notes: This form assumes the oscillator starts at maximum displacement (t = 0); omega is in radians per second and time t in seconds. The result ranges between +A and −A.

name: Kinetic energy from momentum
description: Computes the kinetic energy of a mass m from its momentum p, as p²/(2m). The result is the energy of motion in joules.
notes: Equivalent to ½mv² since p = mv; useful when momentum is known instead of speed. Momentum in kg·m/s and mass in kilograms give joules.

name: Efficiency
description: Computes the efficiency of a machine or process as the useful power output divided by the total power input, expressed as a percentage. The result shows what fraction of input becomes useful output.
notes: The result is already scaled to a percentage, so no further multiplication is needed; it cannot exceed 100 percent for a real device. Both inputs must use the same units.

name: Work-energy theorem
description: Computes the net work done on a mass m from its change in kinetic energy, as ½m(vf² − vi²) between final and initial speeds. The result is the net work in joules.
notes: By the work-energy theorem this equals the total work by all forces; the result is negative when the object slows down. Speeds are in m/s.

name: Elastic collision final velocity
description: Computes the final velocity of body 1 after a one-dimensional elastic collision, from the two masses and their initial velocities, as ((m1−m2)u1 + 2m2·u2)/(m1+m2). The result is in metres per second.
notes: Valid only for perfectly elastic one-dimensional collisions, where both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved. Velocities are signed by direction.

name: Centre of mass (two bodies)
description: Computes the position of the centre of mass of two bodies from their masses and positions, as (m1·x1 + m2·x2)/(m1+m2). The result is the balance-point position in metres.
notes: Positions are measured along one axis from a common origin and may be negative. The centre of mass lies closer to the heavier body.

name: SHM maximum velocity
description: Computes the maximum speed of a simple-harmonic oscillator, reached at the equilibrium point, as the product of angular frequency omega and amplitude a. The result is in metres per second.
notes: Angular frequency omega must be in radians per second; this peak speed occurs as the oscillator passes through equilibrium, where displacement is zero.

name: SHM maximum acceleration
description: Computes the maximum acceleration of a simple-harmonic oscillator, reached at maximum displacement, as ω²a for angular frequency omega and amplitude a. The result is in m/s².
notes: Angular frequency omega must be in radians per second; this peak acceleration occurs at the extremes of motion and points back toward equilibrium.

name: Gravitational potential energy (general)
description: Gives the gravitational potential energy of two point masses separated by distance r, taking the zero of energy at infinite separation. The result is negative because gravity is attractive, and it grows less negative as the masses move apart.
notes: This is the general form for any separation, not the near-surface mgh approximation. Use consistent SI units; r is the center-to-center distance, and the negative sign is physical, not an error.

name: Centripetal force
description: Computes the net inward force required to keep a mass m moving in a circle of radius r at speed v. The force scales with the square of the speed and inversely with the radius, always pointing toward the center of the circle.
notes: This is the required net force, not an extra force to add. Use tangential speed for v; doubling the speed quadruples the needed force.

name: Centripetal acceleration
description: Gives the center-directed acceleration of an object moving in a circle of radius r at speed v. It equals v squared divided by r, representing the constant change of velocity direction even when the speed is steady.
notes: Present even at constant speed, since only the direction of velocity changes. Use the instantaneous tangential speed for v and keep radius in meters.

name: Weight
description: Computes the weight, the gravitational force on a mass m in a gravitational field of strength g. On Earth g is about 9.81 m/s squared, so a 70 kg mass weighs roughly 687 newtons.
notes: Weight is a force in newtons, not a mass in kilograms. The value of g varies with location and altitude and differs on other planets.

name: Torque
description: Calculates the torque produced by a force f applied at a lever arm r, where theta is the angle between the force and the arm. Torque is maximal at 90 degrees (sin = 1) and zero when the force is aligned with the arm.
notes: The angle theta must be in radians. Torque measures rotational effect; only the force component perpendicular to the lever arm contributes.

name: Angular momentum
description: Gives the angular momentum of a rotating rigid body as the product of its moment of inertia i and angular velocity omega. It is the rotational analog of linear momentum and is conserved when no external torque acts.
notes: Angular velocity should be in rad/s and moment of inertia about the same axis of rotation. This form applies to rigid-body rotation about a fixed axis.

name: Rotational kinetic energy
description: Computes the kinetic energy stored in a rotating body from its moment of inertia i and angular velocity omega. It mirrors the linear form (half m v squared), with the energy scaling as the square of the angular velocity.
notes: Angular velocity must be in rad/s, not revolutions per second. The moment of inertia depends on the axis and the mass distribution of the body.

name: Rotational power
description: Gives the mechanical power delivered by a torque acting on a body rotating at angular velocity omega. It is the rotational counterpart of force times velocity, so power rises with both the applied torque and the rotation rate.
notes: Angular velocity must be in rad/s to yield watts; convert from rpm if needed (multiply rpm by 2π/60). Valid for a torque applied about the rotation axis.

name: Total energy of SHM
description: Calculates the total mechanical energy of a simple harmonic oscillator such as a mass on a spring, from the spring constant k and amplitude a. This energy stays constant during the motion, continually shifting between kinetic and potential forms.
notes: Amplitude is the maximum displacement from equilibrium, in meters. The result assumes no damping or friction, so energy is conserved throughout each cycle.

name: Coefficient of restitution
description: Measures the elasticity of a collision as the ratio of the relative speed of separation after impact to the relative speed of approach before it. A value of 1 is a perfectly elastic collision, while 0 is perfectly inelastic.
notes: Use consistent signed velocities along the line of impact; the result is dimensionless and normally lies between 0 and 1. Order the velocity differences consistently to keep the sign positive.

name: Moment of Inertia — Solid Sphere
description: Computes the moment of inertia of a uniform solid sphere about an axis through its center as two-fifths of mass times radius squared. It quantifies the sphere's resistance to angular acceleration.
notes: Assumes a uniform-density solid sphere rotating about a central axis. Result is in kg·m² with mass in kg and radius in meters.

name: Moment of Inertia — Hollow Sphere (Thin Shell)
description: Computes the moment of inertia of a thin spherical shell about a central axis as two-thirds of mass times radius squared. A hollow shell resists rotation more than a solid sphere of equal mass and radius.
notes: Assumes a thin shell with all mass at the surface radius; a thick-walled sphere differs. Result is in kg·m² with mass in kg and radius in meters.

name: Moment of Inertia — Solid Cylinder / Disk
description: Computes the moment of inertia of a uniform solid cylinder or disk about its central symmetry axis as one-half of mass times radius squared. It measures resistance to spinning about that axis.
notes: Applies to rotation about the central longitudinal axis; a diameter axis gives a different value. Length does not appear, and the result is in kg·m².

name: Moment of Inertia — Thin Hoop / Ring
description: Computes the moment of inertia of a thin hoop or ring about its central axis as mass times radius squared. With all mass at the rim, it has the largest inertia of the common shapes for a given mass and radius.
notes: Assumes all mass concentrated at radius r and rotation about the axis perpendicular to the hoop's plane through its center. Result is in kg·m².

name: Moment of Inertia — Thick Hollow Cylinder
description: Computes the moment of inertia of a thick-walled hollow cylinder (annular tube) about its central axis as one-half of mass times the sum of the inner and outer radii squared. It accounts for both wall radii.
notes: Both radii must use the same units, with inner radius less than outer. Setting the inner radius to zero recovers the solid-cylinder result; the answer is in kg·m².

name: Moment of Inertia — Solid Cone (About Axis)
description: Gives the mass moment of inertia of a solid cone about its central symmetry axis, equal to 3/10 times the mass times the base radius squared. It measures how strongly the cone resists angular acceleration about that axis.
notes: The axis passes through the apex along the cone's centerline; r is the base radius, not the slant length. Result units are kg·m² and grow with the square of the radius.

name: Moment of Inertia — Rod About Center
description: Computes the moment of inertia of a thin uniform rod rotating about an axis through its center and perpendicular to its length, equal to (1/12)·m·l². It quantifies rotational inertia for that central axis.
notes: Valid for a thin rod where thickness is negligible; l is the full length. Rotation about the end instead uses (1/3)·m·l², four times larger.

name: Moment of Inertia — Rod About End
description: Computes the moment of inertia of a thin uniform rod rotating about an axis through one end and perpendicular to its length, equal to (1/3)·m·l². This is the value used for a rod pivoting at its tip.
notes: l is the full rod length and the axis is at one end, not the center. This inertia is four times the central-axis value (1/12)·m·l².

name: Moment of Inertia — Rectangular Plate (Central Axis)
description: Gives the moment of inertia of a thin rectangular plate about the axis through its center and perpendicular to its face, equal to (1/12)·m·(a²+b²) where a and b are the two side lengths. It measures resistance to spinning about that central axis.
notes: The axis is perpendicular to the plate through its centroid; thickness is assumed negligible. Both side lengths contribute, each squared and summed.

name: Moment of Inertia — Disk About Diameter
description: Computes the moment of inertia of a thin uniform disk about an axis lying along one of its diameters (in the plane of the disk), equal to (1/4)·m·r². It applies when the disk tips about a line through its center.
notes: This is the diameter (in-plane) axis, giving (1/4)·m·r², which is half the perpendicular central-axis value (1/2)·m·r². Assumes a thin disk.

name: Radius of Gyration
description: Returns the radius of gyration, the distance from the rotation axis at which the whole mass could be concentrated to give the same moment of inertia, computed as the square root of I divided by m. It summarizes how mass is distributed relative to the axis.
notes: I must be taken about the same axis of interest and be in kg·m² with m in kg; the result is a length in meters. It is not a physical radius of the body.

name: Parallel Axis Theorem
description: Applies the parallel axis theorem to find the moment of inertia about an axis parallel to one through the center of mass: I = Icm + m·d², where d is the distance between the two axes. It shifts a known central inertia to any parallel axis.
notes: The two axes must be parallel, and Icm must be about the center-of-mass axis. Moving away from the center of mass always increases inertia, since m·d² is added.

name: Torque from Angular Acceleration
description: Computes the net torque required to give a rotating body an angular acceleration, using the rotational form of Newton's second law, τ = I·α. The result is the turning effort in newton-meters.
notes: I and α must be about the same axis; α is in rad/s². This assumes a rigid body with constant moment of inertia about that axis.

name: Angular Acceleration from Torque
description: Solves the rotational Newton's second law for angular acceleration, α = τ / I, giving how quickly the angular velocity changes under an applied torque. The result is in rad/s².
notes: Torque and moment of inertia must refer to the same axis; a larger inertia yields a smaller acceleration for the same torque.

name: Rolling Kinetic Energy (Total)
description: Adds the translational kinetic energy (1/2)·m·v² and the rotational kinetic energy (1/2)·I·ω² to give the total kinetic energy of a rolling body. It captures energy in both linear motion and spin.
notes: For rolling without slipping the speeds are linked by v = ω·r; enter consistent values. I is about the body's own rotation axis and ω is in rad/s.

name: Flywheel Energy from RPM
description: Computes the rotational kinetic energy stored in a flywheel from its moment of inertia and rotational speed in rpm, converting to angular velocity as ω = 2π·n/60 and evaluating (1/2)·I·ω². The result is the stored energy in joules.
notes: Input speed n is in rpm and is converted internally; do not pre-convert to rad/s. Energy scales with the square of the speed, so doubling rpm quadruples the energy.

name: Angular Velocity (Kinematics)
description: Gives the angular velocity after time t under constant angular acceleration, ω = ω0 + α·t, the rotational analogue of v = v0 + a·t. The result is the final angular velocity in rad/s.
notes: Valid only for constant angular acceleration. Keep ω0 and α in the same rotational sense; a negative α represents deceleration.

name: Angular Displacement (Kinematics)
description: Computes the angle swept in time t under constant angular acceleration, θ = ω0·t + (1/2)·α·t², the rotational analogue of the linear displacement equation. The result is the angular displacement in radians.
notes: Assumes constant angular acceleration and consistent rotational sense for ω0 and α. θ is a total swept angle in radians, not reduced to within one revolution.

name: Final Angular Velocity (No Time)
description: Finds the final angular velocity after turning through angle θ under constant angular acceleration without needing the time, using ω = √(ω0² + 2·α·θ). It is the rotational analogue of v² = v0² + 2·a·s.
notes: Requires constant angular acceleration; θ is in radians and α in rad/s². The radicand must be non-negative, so strong deceleration over a large angle can make this invalid.

name: Centripetal Acceleration (Angular)
description: Computes the centripetal (radial) acceleration of a point moving in a circle from its angular velocity and radius, a = ω²·r. This acceleration points toward the center and keeps the point on its circular path.
notes: ω must be in rad/s, not rpm or degrees. This gives only the radial component; any tangential acceleration from changing speed is separate.

name: Centripetal Acceleration from RPM
description: Computes centripetal acceleration for a body rotating at n rpm at radius r by converting to angular velocity ω = 2π·n/60 and evaluating ω²·r. The result is the inward radial acceleration in m/s².
notes: Input speed n is in rpm and converted internally; do not pre-convert. Acceleration rises with the square of rpm, so it grows quickly at high speeds.

name: Rolling Without Slipping
description: Gives the linear speed of the center of a wheel that rolls without slipping, v = ω·r, linking spin rate to travel speed. The contact point is momentarily at rest, so the center moves at exactly ω·r.
notes: Valid only when there is no slipping between wheel and surface. ω must be in rad/s; the same relation gives the contact-point tangential speed.

name: Tangential Acceleration
description: Computes the tangential acceleration of a point on a rotating body from its angular acceleration and radius, a = α·r. This is the along-the-path component that changes the point's speed.
notes: α must be in rad/s². This is distinct from centripetal acceleration ω²·r; the total acceleration combines both components at right angles.

name: Banking Angle of a Curve
description: Finds the ideal banking angle for a curve so that no friction is needed at speed v, θ = arctan(v²/(r·g)), where r is the curve radius and g is gravity. At this angle the horizontal component of the normal force supplies the centripetal force.
notes: The result is in radians and assumes friction-free ideal banking at exactly speed v. Use consistent SI units; at other speeds some friction is required.

name: Gyroscopic Precession Rate
description: Computes the precession angular velocity of a spinning gyroscope under gravity, Ω = m·g·d/(I·ω), where d is the pivot-to-center-of-mass distance and I·ω is the spin angular momentum. It gives how fast the spin axis slowly circles about the vertical.
notes: Valid in the fast-spin approximation where spin ω is much larger than the precession rate. I is the spin-axis moment of inertia and ω is in rad/s.

name: Physical Pendulum Period
description: Computes the small-oscillation period of a physical (rigid-body) pendulum, T = 2π·√(I/(m·g·d)), where I is the moment of inertia about the pivot and d is the pivot-to-center-of-mass distance. It gives the time for one full swing.
notes: Valid only for small-amplitude swings, and I must be taken about the pivot axis, not the center of mass. Larger amplitudes have longer periods than this predicts.

name: Torque from Force and Angle
description: Computes the torque produced by a force applied at a lever arm, τ = r·F·sin(θ), where θ is the angle between the lever arm and the force direction. Only the perpendicular component of the force creates turning effect.
notes: θ must be in radians; torque is maximal at θ = π/2 (90°) and zero when the force is along the arm. Result is in newton-meters.

name: Work Done by Torque
description: Computes the rotational work done by a constant torque acting through an angular displacement, W = τ·θ, the rotational analogue of force times distance. The result is energy in joules.
notes: θ must be in radians, and the torque is assumed constant over the rotation. For a full turn θ = 2π; a varying torque would require integration.

name: Tangential Force from Torque
description: Finds the tangential force at radius r that produces a given torque, F = τ/r, assuming the force acts perpendicular to the radius. It is the effective force at the rim for a known turning moment.
notes: Assumes the force is applied perpendicular to the lever arm at radius r. A larger radius gives a smaller required force for the same torque.

name: Lever — Effort Force
description: Computes the effort force needed to balance a load on a lever, F = load·(load arm)/(effort arm), from the principle of moments. A longer effort arm relative to the load arm reduces the required effort.
notes: This is the ideal (frictionless, weightless-lever) balance value; real levers need slightly more. Both arm lengths are measured from the fulcrum.

name: Inclined Plane — Effort Force
description: Computes the effort force to move a load up a frictionless inclined plane, F = load·h/l, where h is the height gained and l is the slope length. The incline trades a smaller force over a longer distance.
notes: Ideal frictionless result and it assumes the effort acts parallel to the slope. The load here is a weight in newtons; friction would increase the real effort.

name: Inclined Plane — Mechanical Advantage
description: Gives the ideal mechanical advantage of an inclined plane as the ratio of slope length to height, MA = l/h. It shows how many times the effort force is multiplied compared with lifting straight up.
notes: This is the ideal, frictionless mechanical advantage; friction lowers the actual value. The result is a dimensionless ratio greater than one for a genuine ramp.

name: Wheel and Axle — Effort Force
description: Computes the effort force applied at the wheel to raise a load on the axle, F = load·(axle radius)/(wheel radius), from the balance of torques. A larger wheel radius relative to the axle reduces the effort needed.
notes: Ideal frictionless value; the ratio of radii equals the mechanical advantage. Effort is applied at the wheel rim and the load hangs from the axle.

name: Screw / Jack — Effort Force
description: Computes the ideal effort force at the handle of a screw jack, F = load·p/(2π·r), where p is the thread pitch and r is the handle radius. One turn moves the load by one pitch while the effort travels 2π·r.
notes: Ideal frictionless value; real screw jacks lose much of this advantage to friction (which also provides self-locking). Pitch p and radius r must be in the same length units.

name: Wedge — Mechanical Advantage
description: Gives the ideal mechanical advantage of a wedge as the ratio of its slope length to its thickness, MA = l/t. A long, thin wedge multiplies the driving force more strongly.
notes: Ideal, frictionless ratio; friction (needed to keep a wedge in place) reduces the real advantage. The result is a dimensionless ratio.

name: Pulley System — Effort Force
description: Computes the effort force in an ideal block-and-tackle, F = load/n, where n is the number of rope segments supporting the load. Sharing the load across more segments lowers the pull required.
notes: Ideal frictionless, weightless-rope value; count only the rope segments that actually support the moving load. Real systems need more effort due to friction.

name: Gear Train Ratio
description: Computes the gear ratio of a simple gear train as the number of driven-gear teeth divided by driver-gear teeth, i = Tout/Tin. A ratio above one means torque is multiplied and output speed reduced.
notes: The result is dimensionless; output speed is divided and torque multiplied by this same ratio (ideal, lossless). Tooth counts are whole numbers.

name: Gear Output Speed
description: Computes the output angular speed of a gear pair from the input speed and tooth counts, ωout = ωin·Tin/Tout. A larger driven gear (more teeth) turns more slowly than the driver.
notes: Ideal, lossless relation; the output keeps the input's angular units (here rad/s). Torque changes inversely, rising as speed falls.

name: Belt / Pulley Surface Speed
description: Computes the surface (belt) speed at the rim of a pulley from its diameter and rotational speed in rpm, v = π·d·n/60. This is the linear speed of the belt running over the pulley.
notes: Speed n is in rpm and converted internally; d is the diameter, not the radius. The /60 converts revolutions per minute to per second.

name: Belt Drive — Driven Speed
description: Computes the rotational speed of the driven pulley in a belt drive, n2 = n1·d1/d2, from the driver speed and the two pulley diameters. A larger driven pulley turns more slowly than the driver.
notes: Assumes no belt slip; output speed keeps the input rpm units. Diameters may be replaced by radii since only their ratio matters.

name: Tipping / Toppling Angle
description: Computes the tilt angle at which an object begins to topple, θ = arctan(b/h), where b is the half base width and h is the center-of-mass height. Beyond this angle the vertical through the center of mass falls outside the base.
notes: The result is in radians and assumes tipping about a base edge with no sliding. A wider base or lower center of mass raises the toppling angle.

name: Center of Mass — Two Bodies
description: Computes the position of the center of mass of two point masses along a line, x = (m1·x1 + m2·x2)/(m1 + m2). It is the mass-weighted average of the two positions.
notes: Positions are measured on a common axis and may be negative; the result lies between x1 and x2, nearer the heavier mass. Extends to more bodies by adding terms.

name: Terminal Velocity
description: Finds the steady falling speed at which drag force balances gravity for an object in a fluid, as the square root of two times mass times gravity divided by the product of fluid density, cross-sectional area and drag coefficient. The result is in meters per second.
notes: Applies to the constant-velocity limit where net force is zero, using a fixed drag coefficient. Heavier or more compact objects reach higher terminal speeds; denser fluids reduce it.

name: Free-Fall Time from Height
description: Computes the time t for an object to fall a height h from rest under constant gravitational acceleration g, using t = √(2h/g), derived from h = ½gt².
notes: Assumes free fall from rest with no air resistance. h and g must use consistent units (e.g., meters and m/s²) for t to come out in seconds.

name: Angular Frequency of a Spring-Mass Oscillator (SHM)
description: Calculates the angular frequency of a mass oscillating on an ideal spring in simple harmonic motion. It depends only on the spring's stiffness and the oscillating mass, not on the amplitude of the motion. This is a foundational result used to find the period and frequency of the oscillator.
notes: Assumes an ideal massless spring, no friction or air resistance, and motion within the spring's elastic (Hookean) limit.

name: Angular Frequency of a Simple Pendulum (SHM)
description: Calculates the angular frequency of a simple pendulum undergoing small-angle oscillations. It depends only on the local gravitational acceleration and the pendulum's length, making it independent of both mass and amplitude.
notes: Valid only for small oscillation angles (typically under about 15°), where sin(θ) ≈ θ; treats the pendulum as a point mass on a massless, inextensible string.

name: Perfectly Inelastic Collision — Common Final Velocity
description: Computes the common final velocity of two objects that collide and stick together in a perfectly inelastic collision. It follows directly from conservation of linear momentum for the combined system.
notes: Applies to one-dimensional collisions with a sign convention where velocities in the same direction share the same sign; no external forces act during the collision.

name: Recoil Velocity from Explosive Separation
description: Determines the velocity of one fragment produced when a single body at a known velocity splits into two pieces (e.g. an explosion or decay), given the mass and resulting velocity of the other fragment. It is derived from conservation of momentum for the system before and after separation.
notes: One-dimensional momentum conservation only; assumes no external forces act during the (near-instantaneous) separation event.

name: Atwood Machine Acceleration
description: Calculates the common magnitude of acceleration of the two hanging masses in an ideal Atwood machine, connected over a pulley by an inextensible string. The heavier mass accelerates downward while the lighter mass accelerates upward at the same rate.
notes: Assumes a massless, frictionless pulley, a massless inextensible string, and no air resistance; enter the heavier mass as m1 to obtain a positive result.

name: Atwood Machine String Tension
description: Calculates the tension in the connecting string of an ideal Atwood machine while the system is accelerating. The tension is the same throughout the string on both sides of the frictionless pulley.
notes: Assumes a massless, frictionless pulley and a massless inextensible string; the tension is always less than the weight of the heavier mass and greater than the weight of the lighter mass when m1 ≠ m2.

name: Kinetic Energy Lost in a Perfectly Inelastic Collision
description: Calculates the amount of kinetic energy converted to other forms (heat, sound, deformation) when two objects collide and stick together. It is expressed in terms of the reduced mass of the two-body system and their relative velocity before impact.
notes: Valid for one-dimensional perfectly inelastic collisions only; the result is always non-negative since kinetic energy can only decrease (or stay the same) in such a collision.

name: Total Mechanical Energy of a Circular Orbit
description: Calculates the total mechanical energy (kinetic plus gravitational potential) of a small body in a stable circular orbit around a much larger central mass. The result is always negative, reflecting that the orbiting body is gravitationally bound to the central body.
notes: Assumes a perfectly circular orbit and a two-body system where m2 does not significantly affect the motion of m1 (m1 ≫ m2); ignores relativistic effects and atmospheric drag.
